newsitem.title: UK: London tube sale plans "may come this week"-paper.
newsitem.headline: London tube sale plans "may come this week"-paper.

text.p: A secret plan to privatise the London Underground may be revealed this week, to link in with a pre-election privatisation theme, according to a front-page report in The Sunday Times newspaper.
The scheme was revealed in confidential minutes from last week's cabinet summit at Chequers which were leaked to The Sunday Times, the report said.
A Department of Transport spokesman told Reuters on Sunday no decision on privatisation of the London Underground had yet been made. He said he could not comment on purportedly leaked documents.
"It is true to say that the government is examining the potential for applying the principles of privatisation to the London Underground, but no decision has yet been made," he said.

He said the newspaper report neglected to state there would be a hefty regime to put caps on fares. "Whereas the Sunday Times piece offers the opinion that actually there would be no controls on fares whatsoever...it is yet to be decided."
The report said fares would be allowed to rise by more than inflation before the sell-off and that services may be cut afterwards.

The Sunday Times said the privatisation may raise only 600 million pounds for taxpayers, "even though the network is worth billions of pounds". It said the Tube's network was valued at 13 billion pounds but the government said it would raise a maximum of 1.4 billion with proceeds as low as 600 million pounds.

It quoted Labour's deputy leader, John Prescott, as saying: "This is dogma gone mad. The public will be appalled that the Underground is being sold at a knock-down price, and that ministers are admitting privately it could lead to higher prices and fewer routes."

It said Transport Secretary George Young was so worried he wanted the Treasury rather than his department to make good the shortfall if the subsidy needed to sell the Underground is greater than the net proceeds.

The report said Young said the options included selling the Underground as a single business, the sale or franchising of lines or groups of lines with trains, track and possibly stations included, and setting up a track authority to own the network while individual lines or groups of them are franchised.
Meanwhile Young, although refusing to comment on the leak, told GMTV's Sunday programme his department was studying the privatisation of the London Underground today.
"We are seeing whether the real improvements we are seeing on the railways can be applied to London Underground."
